title: Lesson 25: The Power User's Mental Model: Judging a Tool's Reliability
description: Judging a tool's reliability before you build on it: what reliability and availability mean, how to tell an SLO from an SLA, the signals that separate a dependable tool from a fragile one, and how to weigh a vendor's track record against its promises.

questions.question: Priya is choosing between two tools for her weekly client report. A new tool with heavy marketing promises "99.9 percent uptime" and an "SLA," but its status page shows almost no history and no post-mortems, while the model she already uses has months of documented incident history she has watched and logged. Per the lesson, why should the new tool's empty status page give her pause?
options: Because an empty incident history means she has no track record to grade, so she would be trusting a promise with no evidence behind it
Because a short status page history is proof the tool is deliberately hiding a major outage
Because any tool that has not been through an outage is fragile and guaranteed to fail soon
Because the vendor's "99.9 percent uptime" figure contradicts the empty status page, so the tool is actively lying
questions.explanation: The lesson says an empty incident history is not proof a tool is fragile, but it is proof you have no evidence either way, which means you would be trusting a promise with nothing behind it. A power user grades a tool by its track record, not by assuming the best from a missing one.

questions.question: A vendor advertises "99.9 uptime" for its API. When Priya reads the fine print, missing the number earns an apology rather than a refund or credit. Based on the lesson, how should she classify this promise?
options: It is an SLO, a target value that carries no explicit consequence when missed, even though it is advertised as an SLA
It is an SLA, because the vendor put a specific percentage in writing
It is an SLI, because it is a measurable number like error rate or uptime
It is an error budget, because it tells her how much downtime the vendor is allowed
questions.explanation: The lesson gives the test: ask what happens if the number is missed. If the answer is a payout or penalty, it is an SLA; if it is just an apology, it is an SLO. A percentage in writing does not make it an SLA against the lesson's rule. An SLI is the measured indicator, and an error budget is the allowed amount of failure built into a target.

questions.question: Priya's weekly client report runs once a day and a notification can wait. Per the lesson's reliability-to-task matching, what should she conclude about the reliability she actually needs?
options: She does not need a 99.999 percent service, and chasing one would cost her time and budget she does not have
She should require the most reliable tool available, since any downtime is unacceptable for a client report
She should abandon any tool below 99.9 percent availability, because that is the only acceptable standard
She should trust the newest tool regardless of its track record, because novelty implies better reliability
questions.explanation: The lesson, drawing on Google SRE's rule that a service should be made reliable enough but no more reliable than it needs to be, says Priya does not need extreme availability for a weekly report and that chasing it costs time and budget. The right move is to match the tool's reliability (and her fallback) to what the workflow actually needs.
